lesson.title: Commands in the Wild
lesson.subtitle: Recipes, dialogues and the register switch — where German commands go native

hook.title: The Recipe's Dirty Secret
hook.content: Open a German cookbook and the commands get lazier — and more ancient. Real recipes skip the pronoun and often the finiteness too: Wasser kochen, Tee machen, Brot essen — 'water to-boil, tea to-make, bread to-eat.' That bare infinitive parade is a command with the stem exposed, the same stripped form you drilled as Komm! — just wearing its infinitive coat. English recipes do the mirror move: 'boil water, add salt, stir.' The command is the oldest sentence shape humans own, and in the wild — recipes, signs, dialogues — German simply lets it run.

footnotes.title: bitte — the Softener
footnotes.content: Bitte (please — literally 'ask/bid', the twin hiding in English bid) converts any command from order to request: Komm! vs Komm, bitte! English once did the same with pray: 'pray come in' → 'prithee' → modern please. Both languages ask politely by mentioning the asking.

pattern.title: Two Registers, One Stem
pattern.content: Friend register: Komm! Trink Tee! Iss Brot! — bare-stem commands, chained with und: Komm und iss! Recipe register: Wasser kochen, Tee machen, Kaffee trinken — infinitive-style commands with no pronoun at all, the register of cookbooks and instruction manuals. Formal register: Essen Sie! Trinken Sie! — the verb-first Sie-command. The same stems serve all three: kochen, essen, trinken, machen, kommen, suchen — switch audience, keep the stem. One honest gap: negative commands need nicht, which arrives with topic 12 — komm nicht! waits one topic down the trail.
pattern.linguist_note: The recipe infinitive is a survival of the old Gerundium: medieval German recipes were written as noun-verb pairs ('zu machene' — to make). English once did it too — 'to make a pie: take flour' — before the imperative took over the kitchen.

exercises.prompt: The recipe list — match each step with its reading:
exercises.target_answer: Wasser kochen, Tee machen, Kaffee trinken, Brot essen
exercises.meaning: boil water, make tea, drink coffee, eat bread
exercises.explanation: Recipe style: noun then bare infinitive, no pronoun — a command with the stem exposed.

exercises.prompt: Which line sounds like it came from a German cookbook?
exercises.explanation: Recipes drop the subject entirely: Wasser kochen, Tee machen — the stem parade.

exercises.meaning: drink! tea — drink tea! (to a friend)
exercises.explanation: Bare stem + object: Trink Tee! — the du-command with nothing attached.

exercises.prompt: Formal register (to eat): _____ Sie bitte! (Invite a guest to eat):
exercises.explanation: The Sie-command borrows the they-form: Essen Sie! — essen keeps its e→i vowel only in du (isst) and ihr (esst).

exercises.prompt: Assemble the dialogue line: 'Come and eat bread'
exercises.meaning: Komm und iss Brot = come and eat bread

vocab_hints.note: essen's du-form isst — the command keeps the i

exercises.explanation: Two commands chained with und — and iss keeps its shifted vowel, the stem-changer in action.

summary.outcome: Deploy commands in three registers: friend (Komm!), recipe (Wasser kochen), formal (Essen Sie!).
summary.takeaway: One stem, three registers: Komm! / Wasser kochen / Kommen Sie! — the command is German's oldest sentence shape.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the accusative Him-Case — why only der changes to den, and how English him and whom prove it.

essen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + Ablaut Vowels
essen.context_translation: What do we want to eat?
essen.etymology_derivation: Medial t → ss. Noun: das Essen (food).

trinken.context_translation: I drink a glass of water.

suchen.context_translation: I am looking for my glasses.
suchen.etymology_derivation: k → ch. Direct transitive object without prepositions.

brot.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *braudą — originally "the fermented/risen thing", kin to the verb brew (German brauen). Bread is "the brewed thing". [wiktionary]

ukraine.etymology_derivation: The same name as English Ukraine; shared proper name. [wiktionary]

günstig.context_translation: This hotel is very good value.
günstig.etymology_derivation: Gunst (favor) + -ig; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

geschmack.context_phrase: Der Kuchen hat einen guten Geschmack.
geschmack.context_translation: The cake has a good taste.
geschmack.etymology_derivation: From Old High German gismac, from West Germanic smakku; English smack and smatch are cognates of the same taste root, and the ge prefix has no English counterpart. [wiktionary]

wenig.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wainagaz 'miserable', its vowel blended with Old High German wē, akin to English woe: the woe-word came to mean little, few. [wiktionary]

esel.etymology_derivation: From Old High German esil, from late Proto-West Germanic *asil, borrowed from Late Latin asellus, the diminutive of asinus behind English ass. [wiktionary]

musiker.etymology_derivation: Musik + -er; Musik comes from Latin musica - the same Latin word behind English music and musician. [wiktionary][etymonline]

merken.context_translation: I make a note of your number.
merken.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *markijaną (to mark, notice) — the mark- root behind English mark and remark. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
